---
title: "From climate stresses to system vulnerabilities"
format: html
bibliography: references.bib
link-citations: true
---

Before generating scenarios, the assessment defines its system boundary, planning horizon, performance
indicators and acceptability criteria.
Indicators might describe water-supply reliability, flood levels or environmental-flow deficits.
Thresholds should reflect stakeholder objectives, service standards or ecological requirements.
A change in river discharge alone does not establish whether a system performs acceptably [@brown2012].

The stress test then connects three activities, illustrated in the diagram below.

1. **Generate climate conditions.** Select the climate characteristics that could affect performance and
   vary them systematically over a justified range.
   Changes in mean temperature and precipitation provide a useful starting point, but seasonality,
   rainfall intensity, drought duration or other characteristics may be decisive.
   Perturbed historical records or stochastic weather generators can supply the required time series.
   Multiple realizations help explore different weather sequences under the same prescribed climate change.
2. **Simulate the system response.** Use these time series to drive hydrological and, where needed,
   infrastructure or water-management models.
   Calculate the performance indicators consistently across the experiment.
   This connects climatic stresses to consequences such as shortages, high flows or ecological impacts.
3. **Identify vulnerable conditions.** Relate the indicators to the imposed stresses and compare them
   with the acceptability criteria.
   The result shows where performance deteriorates, which combinations cross a threshold, and which
   stressors or interactions drive those changes.

With two stressors, results can be displayed as a **climate response surface**: temperature change on one
axis, precipitation change on the other, and system performance represented by colour or contours.
A performance threshold divides the surface into acceptable and unacceptable regions.
Several indicators may produce different boundaries, revealing trade-offs between objectives.
Variation among weather realizations can also make the boundary uncertain rather than a single sharp line
[@fowler2024].
